paper_title: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order. We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family. We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance. In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC. LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Many distinct algorithms are built from the same set of computational primitives, composed in different orders to implement different behaviors. For example, database query engine can combine operations such as filtering, joining, sorting, and aggregation in different sequences depending on the query being executed. Modular programming lets the same reusable components be dynamically composed for many purposes within single codebase. Transformer language models lack this flexibility; their layers are executed in fixed, predefined order for every input. This rigidity may make these models less efficient, since useful computational primitives may need to be represented repeatedly at different depths. Prior work has focused on increasing the sparsity of models using mixture of experts (MoE) (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022) or reusing layers multiple times during the forward pass in looped models (Dehghani et al., 2018; Lan et al., 2019; Geiping et al., 2026). Other work has investigated skipping layers dynamically during the forward pass (Elhoushi et al., 2024; Raposo et al., 2024; Bae et al., 2025). However, all of these approaches still enforce the order in which the layers of the model must be executed. In this paper, we introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture in which small router, trained end-to-end without explicit supervision, dynamically selects the next layer from global library of transformer blocks. sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 1: We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), novel architecture where the next executed transformer layer is chosen at runtime. We use strided window attention within the routed core to allow information to flow through the sequence dimension while using the same attention and MLP parameters for all tokens within each window. layers to remain inactive on given forward pass. By changing only the library size, LoL therefore spans continuum from highly reused, dense computation to highly sparse computation. We visualize our novel architecture in Figure 1. Dynamic layer selection introduces challenge. We want to allow different token positions the flexibility to select different layer orderings, but this means that vector at one token position extracted by selected attention layer might attend to vectors at previous token positions extracted by different selected attention layers. We observe that this mismatch makes training unstable and harms performance. At the same time, if we chose single layer ordering for the entire context, we would risk either breaking causality or making layer decisions with too little information (only the prompt). We therefore introduce windowed attention masking strategy that simultaneously allows different windows to adaptively select layer orderings while also preventing the above mismatch problem and preserving causality. We partition the context into windows, route each window using only information available from earlier windows, and shift the window boundaries across routed depths so that information can propagate between neighboring windows, expanding the field of view with depth. We use synthetic and natural-language experiments to study and interpret our models learned layer orderings. On sudoku and maze tasks, LoL learns distinct layer-ordering patterns for different solution strategies; forcing strategys learned routing path at inference time causes the model to follow that strategy. This phenomenon is especially clear in mazes, where all algorithms we consider use the same output syntax and differ only in the order in which they explore cells. We find that fixing layer ordering controls the cell exploration order itself. In multilingual language modeling, different languages use distinct execution paths, with languages that share scripts exhibiting similar routing patterns. We also train LoL on mix of safe and unsafe data, finding that ridge regression trained on routing features distinguishes these categories on held-out data with high AUROC. On general web text, we vary the library size to induce parameter reuse regimes with FLOPs-to-parameters ratio comparable to that of looped transformers and also to induce sparse regimes with FLOPs-toparameters ratio comparable to MoE models, finding that LoL remains competitive across this range. Finally, at 1B parameters on math data, LoL is competitive with conventional dense transformers in terms of loss and benchmark accuracy in FLOPs-matched setting. These results suggest that layer ordering can become learned part of the computation itself rather than fixed architectural choice. LoL unifies behaviors associated with seemingly distinct dense, depth-recurrent, and MoE models by varying single knob, the size of the layer library, while exposing the models internal execution path. Because routing patterns can be extracted and intervened on, LoL also provides simple mechanism for studying and controlling latent computation. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: We propose Library of Layers (LoL), novel architecture in which router selects blocks to apply from global library of transformer layers, making layer selection, ordering, and the number of times each layer is used conditional on the input. We use maze, sudoku, multilingual, and safety training data to empirically show the LoL router learns input-adaptive patterns from data. Moreover, these router patterns can then be used to control the model at test time by forcing the layer execution ordering. We demonstrate that LoL models perform competitively across spectrum of sparsity levels, from low-sparsity looped models that repeatedly reuse the same layers to high-sparsity mixture of experts models.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Prior architectures reuse parameters across depths or select subset of parameters at each depth. Library of Layers spans both regimes by varying the size of its shared library of transformer blocks. Parameter Sharing. Looped transformers, which repeatedly reuse the same transformer blocks, are efficient and can be made Turing complete (Dehghani et al., 2018; Lan et al., 2019; Giannou et al., 2023; Csordas et al., 2024; Saunshi et al., 2025; McLeish et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2026; Prairie et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026a). Looped transformers have also been studied in the context of synthetic algorithmic tasks, showing they can outperform fixed-depth counterparts in both learning efficiency and accuracy (Giannou et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; McLeish et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2024). Recurrence in other architectural regimes such as graph and convolutional neural networks has also shown promising results (Schwarzschild et al., 2021; Bansal et al., 2022; Ibarz et al., 2022; Schwarzschild, 2023; Bear et al., 2024). Parameter sharing has been explored for many components of the modern transformer architecture, for example, QKV weights and KV caches across layers (Sun et al., 2024; Kayyam et al., 2026). We build on these works by incorporating architectural choices from looped transformers, such as only using recurrence in the middle layers of the model; see Figure 2 (top-left). Most similar to our work is that of Gong et al. (2024). However, Gong et al. (2024) pretrain their model before adding layer reuse and do not dynamically choose each layer in the final model. Gong et al. (2024) use top-k routing with greater than one, unlike our top-1 routing. They avoid attention space mismatches by averaging the raw weights of the selected experts in the attention computation and combine the output of the FFN via weighted mean based on the router output weighting. Routing mechanisms. Mixture of experts (MoE) layers (Shazeer et al., 2017) have become the norm for large transformer-based models (OpenAI, 2025; Xu et al., 2026), often implemented with top-k token-based routing according to the current hidden state. Huang et al. (2026b) extend this to share global pool of experts so that all layers can select any expert. Others add skip option to the router, allowing tokens to dynamically skip layers (Raposo et al., 2024; Bae et al., 2025). Ternovtsii & Bilak (2026) route through multiple smaller transformer layers instead of only routing the MLP, as done in conventional MoE. LoL goes beyond choosing which computation to apply at fixed position in the network: each window selects complete transformer block from library shared across all routed depths, making both block ordering and reuse input-dependent.

sections.title: 3.1 THE LIBRARY
sections.content: The architecture is built from decoder-only transformer blocks (Vaswani et al., 2017), organized into prelude, routed core, and coda. Following prior work on looped transformers (Saunshi et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2026), we use adaptive layer selection only in the middle of our LoL models. The prelude and coda are fixed-order stacks of decoder layers with full causal attention, at the beginning and end of the architecture, respectively. They surround the routed core, which applies blocks selected from library {E1, . . . , EL}. Library size counts the distinct blocks stored, whereas core depth counts the block applications executed. We call each library block an expert and each application routed depth. For example, with = 3 and = 3, the sequence E1 E3 E1 repeats one expert and leaves another unused; we call this sequence routing path.

sections.content: Figure 2: Library of Layers uses strided window attention and top-1 router to allow for efficient training. LoL is made up of prelude, routed core, and coda. The layers in the prelude and coda can attend over the whole sequence. In the core, the sequence is split into windows of tokens, and at every routed depth router selects one layer from the shared library per window (topleft). Attention is restricted to each window, but the window boundaries shift by tokens between successive routed depths, allowing information to flow across windows (Strided Window Attention, top-right). Window 0 has no history, so its router uses the first token and learned vector e(ℓ) for routed depth ℓ (bottom-left). For window > 0, the router averages the mean hidden states of earlier windows 0, . . . , 1 and selects one layer (bottom-right). With = 4 and = 2, Layers 1 and 3 share the same boundaries while Layer 2 is offset, so information can pass between neighboring windows. Token 5 is highlighted in red to show this: in Layer 1 it is the first token in new window, while in Layer 2 its window includes tokens 3 and 4. Different windows of tokens can follow different routing paths, as described below. We visualize our forward pass in Figures 1 and 2, and provide pseudocode in Algorithm 1 in the appendix.

sections.title: 3.2 ROUTING
sections.content: Routing must preserve causality, and the router may only use information that will also be available during generation. The expert selected for token cannot depend on later tokens since that would violate causality. One could select an expert for the whole sequence using only the first token to preserve causality, but this would prevent the layer ordering from adapting to information revealed later in the sequence. Alternatively, routing each token independently could assign neighboring tokens to different experts, each with its own query, key, and value projections. In this case, queries and keys computed on different attention heads would be compared, and we find empirically that this setup leads to training instability and poor performance. To overcome both problems, we chunk the sequence at each depth and route separately for each chunk. We then stride the chunk boundaries every depth to allow information to flow between adjacent chunks, similarly to how the field of view under sliding window attention increases with depth. All tokens in window use the same expert with causal attention restricted to that window, preventing the Q-K mismatch.

sections.title: 3.2.2 THE ROUTER
sections.content: When selecting an expert for each window > 0, the router receives information only from prior windows 0 < to preserve causality. Precisely, the router is linear layer and the input is the mean over windows of the mean hidden state per window. For the first window I0, there are no prior windows to use. We instead input the mean of learned depth-specific vector e(ℓ) and the first tokens hidden state to the router. We show this in Figure 2 (bottom). To train the routed core, we use loss-free load balancing (Wang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024). The selected experts residual update is scaled by its router probability, allowing gradients to flow to the router. Following Shazeer et al. (2017), we add Gaussian noise to the router logits before the softmax to encourage exploration during training. Compared with routing per token in MoE models, routing per window provides coarser training signal: gradient contributions from all tokens in window are aggregated through single shared routing decision, rather than separate decisions for each token. We use FiLM (Perez et al., 2018) to add learned depth-dependent scale and bias after each normalization in the transformer block. We describe our implementation of FiLM in Appendix for completeness. 3.

sections.title: INCREASING DEPTH DURING TRAINING
sections.content: The training cost of LoL is mainly controlled by the routed core depth (D). Small would make training cheap by reducing FLOPs per parameter but would lead to shallower model with poorer performance. Therefore, we begin training with shallow routed core and gradually increase over the course of training. This procedure saves compute by performing much of training with shallower model, but ultimately constructs deep and expressive model for deployment. This growing procedure allows the routers to explore experts quickly and cheaply during early training, as the depth of the model is smaller. This is similar to increasing the number of loops of recurrent model over training (McLeish et al., 2025) or progressive stacking (Gong et al., 2019) when training vanilla transformers. We refer to this technique as growing. Additional architecture and training details are provided in Appendix A. We provide ablations for our design decisions in Appendix B.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We conduct an analysis of LoLs capabilities using range of synthetic and real-world data. We begin by using multilingual text, safety text, and synthetic tasks to trace what LoL learns during training, and we find that the path the model uses is often interpretable in these regimes. Subsequently, we train LoL on mixture of math data, showing LoL can learn to perform language modeling and mathematical reasoning. Finally, we vary the sparsity of LoL models while training on web text and find LoL is competitive with widely used architectures at wide range of sparsities. For our 360M parameter models, we use 4 layers in the prelude, 4 layers in the coda, and depth of 16 in the routed core.

sections.title: 4.1 WHAT ROUTING PATHS ENCODE AND CONTROL
sections.content: We begin by studying the router behavior in four training tasks: multilingual text, safety text, sudoku, and mazes. We first examine whether routing features distinguish languages and safety labels, then intervene on routing paths to control the strategies used to solve sudoku puzzles and mazes.

Left: PCA projection of the routing paths of 360M parameter LoL model trained on an equal mixture of 10 languages. sections.title: 4.1.1 MULTILINGUAL
sections.content: First, we train 360M parameter models on an equal mix of 10 different languages from FineWeb-2 (Penedo et al., 2025) for 10 billion tokens. On held-out validation set, for each sampled window, we encode the routers selected expert at every routed depth as one-hot vector. We then concatenate these one-hot vectors and project the resulting vector into two dimensions using PCA. In Figure 3 (left), we see that the routing paths are reasonably distinct per language and the Latin-script languages all share similar paths. Each point in the plot represents one window and its sequence of selected experts. In Appendix Figure 11, we see LoL gradually learns to distinguish between languages and route them through different computational paths by dynamically reordering the experts in its library over the course of training. Note that the same layers are used for various languages but just executed in different orders.

sections.title: 4.1.2 SAFETY
sections.content: We now ask whether routing probabilities encode safety-relevant information in natural text. Using the harmfulness scores assigned to FineWeb sequences by Maini et al. (2026), we treat score-0 sequences as safe and score-4 and score-5 sequences as unsafe. We train models with the same architecture as our multilingual models for 10B tokens on an equal mixture of safe and unsafe text, without providing the harmfulness labels during training. We train linear ridge regression to predict the sequences harmfulness label from windows router probabilities across all routed depths. We use held out set of 50M tokens for training the linear regression, split into 40M for development and 10M for testing. The probe achieves held-out test set AUROC of 0.92, showing that router probabilities contain linearly accessible information about the datasets harmfulness labels. Because each label applies to an entire sequence, an individual window may not contain the content responsible for that label. We therefore also train sequence-level ridge probe using router probabilities averaged across windows. This probe achieves test set AUROC of 0.95. Appendix C.2 shows that simpler readouts recover much of the predictive signal in routing features, while label shuffling controls yield chance performance.

sections.title: 4.1.3 SUDOKU
sections.content: Next, we analyze forcing routing paths to control the sudoku solving strategy. We train the model with strategy information available only to the router, then extract representative routing path for each strategy. At inference, we remove the strategy information and force the model to follow the corresponding path. We construct our dataset including five sudoku solving strategies, each with its own step syntax, fully described in Table 3 in the appendix. Our data is formatted as : <Input Grid> [Sx] : <Solving Steps> : <Final Grid> <eos>, where [Sx], with {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, identifies the solving strategy used to generate the reasoning trace. As the first window for all inputs is just the sudoku grid, we need the [Sx] identifier to tell the model which algorithm to use at test time. The strategy description tokens are masked from all parts of the network but the router. We train for approximately 10B tokens, computing the loss over only the solving steps and final grid, masking the question and strategy description. For each strategy, we find the mode path by running the trained model with teacher forcing on heldout validation puzzles containing the strategy description. For each window and routed depth, we select the expert with the highest mean router probability across these puzzles and fix its residual weight to that mean. Here, mode refers to the highest mean probability, not the most frequent discrete choice; the path fixes both expert choices and residual weights. We report both the mode paths and how consistently the router agrees with the mode path at each depth in Appendix Figures 13 and 12, respectively. We then test LoL on new sudoku grids, replacing the strategy description with neutral filler, [...], and forcing each window to follow the corresponding mode path for the requested strategy. This tests whether fixing the path is enough to make the model follow that strategy. trajectory is marked correct only if every step is legal, follows the requested strategys syntax and rules, and leads to the correct solution. In Figure 3 (middle), we plot the confusion matrix where we force the mode path for each strategy. We see that the model uses the expected strategy with close to 100% accuracy when the mode path is forced for that strategy. Appendix Figure 14 also shows that LoL solves sudoku puzzles with close to 100% accuracy when given the strategy token [Sx] instead of forcing routing path.

sections.title: 4.2 MATHEMATICAL REASONING AT THE 1B SCALE
sections.content: Next, we scale training to 1B parameters with models that are 16 layers deep. For LoL, we divide the 16 layers into 4 prelude layers, 4 coda layers, and depth of 8 in the routed core. We train on mixture of Nemotron (Mahabadi et al., 2025) and OpenMath (Toshniwal et al., 2024) data. We also grow the LoL models using 1 sqrt schedule for 75% of training, following McLeish et al. (2025). We train for approximately 90 ExaFLOPs; this equates to approximately 20B tokens for the most efficient model. In Figure 4 (left), we see our models are competitive in terms of training loss with the parameter equivalent dense baselines. We use both full attention and sliding window attention as baselines, where we set the size of the sliding window to be equal to the window size in the strided attention in LoL. In Appendix Figure 20 and Table 5, we include comparison to the vanilla model with strided attention. This model performs slightly worse than the vanilla and vanilla sliding window attention models. We note that the math training data is synthetic; therefore, loss values in Figure 4 are lower than the FineWeb ones in other plots. Moreover, in Figure 4 (right), we see our models are learning to use different experts at different routed depths. In this setting, where the library size equals the routed core depth, we see clusters form where experts are often used across neighboring depths. However, some experts are used across wider range of depths. In Table 1, we benchmark the same models on ARC-Easy (Clark et al., 2018), ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), and GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021). We use lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024) and report the standard errors for each benchmark in the table. We use these benchmarks as they are known to provide stronger, more reliable signal at smaller model sizes and token counts (Magnusson et al., 2025; McLeish et al., 2026). We see almost all evaluations are competitive and remain within 2 standard errors of each other on all benchmarks, showing LoL is competitive across range of modern architectures. The only exception is the vanilla model, which scores poorly on ARC-Easy.

sections.title: 4.3 HOW BIG SHOULD YOUR LIBRARY BE?
sections.content: Library size (L) determines how many distinct blocks are available, while core depth (D) determines how many blocks are executed. small library requires reuse; large library allows blocks to remain unused along given routing path. We compare the small-library regime with looped transformers and the large-library regime with sparse MoE models.

sections.title: 4.3.1 COMPARISON TO LOOPED TRANSFORMERS
sections.content: First, we compare to looped transformers. Following the analysis of Huang et al. (2026a), we use the Huginn (Geiping et al., 2026) architecture for our looped model baseline. We compare models at several distinct parameter counts, reusing layers to reach total effective parameter count of 360M . To ensure fair comparison, we fix the library size in our LoL models to match the size of the recurrent block in the Huginn models. We train for 10B tokens of FineWeb data (Penedo et al., 2024). In Figure 5, we see that our LoL models are competitive in terms of loss with the parameter matched looped models. We note that the LoL models have slightly higher variance in final loss over three seeds. We hypothesize this is due to sensitivity to the initialization of the router causing different paths to be explored during training. In Appendix Figure 21, we show the routing diversity for each LoL model shown in Figure 5. Unlike Huginn, LoL can offer sparse behavior by simply scaling the size of its library.

sections.title: 4.3.2 COMPARISON TO SPARSE MIXTURE OF EXPERTS
sections.content: Finally, we compare to sparse mixture of experts models. We compare at 3 : 2 sparsity ratio: the MoE model uses three experts per layer with two active, while LoL uses 24 experts over 16 routed depths. We increase the MoE experts intermediate expansion factor relative to our standard 360M model to match active parameters per token as closely as possible. To align computation, LoL uses MoE prelude and coda layers, and the MoE baseline uses strided attention at the same depths as LoL. We again use growing for the LoL models and train all models for approximately 17 ExaFLOPs; this equates to approximately 10B tokens for the most efficient model. In Figure 6 (left), the MoE baseline achieves slightly lower training loss than LoL, with gap of approximately 0.05 (2.75 vs. 2.8). We note it is common for higher cross-entropy loss to coexist with strong downstream performance in latent reasoning models (Saunshi et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026a). In Figure 6 (right), we visualize the expert utilization across routed depths on an evaluation set. Experts vary in depth specialization: some favor earlier or later depths, while others are used across depths, highlighting the flexibility of LoL models on real-world language modeling data.

sections.title: 5 DISCUSSION
sections.content: LoL generalizes the parameter reuse and sparsity of looped models, standard feedforward transformers, and MoEs into single model family, allowing us to switch between these regimes simply by varying the library size. While our design addresses several challenges we discuss above, this paper is an initial exploration into dynamic layer ordering, and we believe that future work will vastly improve on our design. Moreover, the goal of our experiments is to show not merely that an architecture with dynamic layer ordering can achieve competitive performance, but also that it provides new tool for model interpretability and control over models reasoning strategies. We now enumerate several directions for future work that we believe are especially promising. First, LoL is built with controllability at the core. We see in Figure 3 that we can find distinct routing paths underlying languages and algorithms, and we can intervene on routing paths at inference to control the model. In Section 4.1.2, we show that routing features distinguish safe from unsafe text. Whether such features can also support interventions in chat settings, including behaviors related to lying, scheming, and safety (Park et al., 2024), remains an open question. Next, LoL can in principle employ larger computational depth at inference time than at training time, offering mechanism for test-time scaling and increasing its capacity for latent reasoning. Finally, another promising direction is to combine test-time learning (Chen et al., 2026; Hotsko et al., 2026; Zhao & Jones, 2026) with our top-1 routing. For example, instead of routing over full transformer blocks, one may route over growing library of test-time learnable adapters for each layer. This approach would allow the parametric memory to be available to all layers of the model.

sections.title: A ADDITIONAL ARCHITECTURE AND TRAINING DETAILS
sections.content: Given core depth of D, library of experts, and an input sequence n, these three groups produce the output probabilities RnV as shown in Algorithm 1. Our main experiments are conducted at the 360M parameter scale based on the GPT-2 Medium architecture (Radford et al., 2019). Unlike GPT-2, our models use RoPE (Su et al., 2024), RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019), SwiGLU MLPs (Shazeer, 2020), and bias free attention (Chowdhery et al., 2023). Our 1B model shape is based upon the Llama-3.2-1b shape (Meta, 2024), using the same architecture as the 360M model. We use the GPT-NeoX tokenizer (Black et al., 2022) for our predominantly English FineWeb training experiments and the larger OLMo3 (Olmo et al., 2025) tokenizer for our multilingual experiments. For our toy sudoku and maze experiments, we use small tokenizers specifically for the vocabulary of each task. For natural language experiments, we use = 128 and = 64, with total context length of 1024 tokens. For sudoku and mazes, we set the first window to span the question and strategy description. Subsequent windows use = 128 and = 64 for sudoku, and = 64 and = 32 for mazes. To train the router, we use loss-free load balancing (Wang et al., 2024), adding per-expert bias only for expert selection, ρk = arg maxm (ak,m + bm) , where ak,m is the softmax probability of expert before adding the balancing bias. We weight the selected expert using this probability, αk = ak,ρk . As in MoE routing (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022), this retains differentiable path from the loss to the router through αk, without differentiating through the discrete selection. For our LoL models, we apply learned, depth-dependent scale and bias after each normalization in the transformer block. Specifically, in place of the regular normalization in the transformer block, we use: γs Norms(x) + βs, {attn, ffn}, where γ and β are depth-dependent.

sections.content: We use the Muon optimizer (Jordan et al., 2024) with AdamW (Kingma & Ba, 2014; Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017). We use document blocked attention, meaning that tokens in one document never attend to tokens in another document in any experiment.
